cur:catacombs2-saint-maximin-sidoine.summary: Five arcades on spiral-fluted columns frame scenes of Christ's ministry around a damaged central niche, where two soldiers once kept watch beneath a jewelled cross. To the left Christ lays his hand on the eyes of a small blind man; to the right he foretells Peter's denial, the cockerel at their feet; at either end he heals a small male and a kneeling female petitioner. The lid adds Christ giving the keys to Peter, a raising of the dead and the multiplication of the loaves, flanking a blank panel held by winged genii.
facts: Medieval tradition held that it received the remains of Saint Sidonius; the scene of the healing of the blind man was linked with him and gave the tomb its name.

Father Lacordaire later told how monks, fearing Saracen raids around 710, swapped the bodies of Mary Magdalene and Sidonius between their sarcophagi to protect the saint's relics; the story is a legend, not documented history.
The crypt's four sarcophagi are dated to about the end of the 4th century, and several were probably carved in Arles from imported marble.
cur:catacombs2-saint-maximin-sidoine.notes: The two miracles at the ends are not securely identified (proposals include the centurion's servant, the Canaanite woman, or the woman with an issue of blood).

cur:objects-coin-anonymous-follis-class-.summary: This large bronze coin bears no emperor's portrait or name: the obverse shows the bust of Christ with a cross-nimbus, blessing and holding a Gospel book, with IC XC and the name EMMANOUEL, and the reverse carries only the words 'Jesus Christ, King of Kings' in four lines. Everyday coins like this put the image and confession of Christ into the hands of ordinary people across the Byzantine world. Worn by circulation, this specimen still shows the calm face of the Lord.
facts: Wikipedia's article on Byzantine coinage explains that in the 10th century 'anonymous folles' were struck instead of coins depicting the emperor, with the bust of Christ and the inscription meaning 'Jesus Christ, Emperor of Emperors'.
Ghent University Library's catalogue reads the obverse legend as EMMANOUEL and the reverse as IhSUS XRISTUS bASILEU bASILE, and dates this Class A2 specimen to about 976–1030.

cur:objects2-old-kilcullen-west-shaft.summary: The shaft of the west cross at Old Kilcullen stands without its head among the ruins of an early monastery. On its west face, according to Peter Harbison's reading, the panels show from top to bottom a horseman, Samson slaying the lion, and Christ entering Jerusalem. The simplified relief is typical of the granite crosses of the Barrow valley.
facts: The panel identifications follow Peter Harbison's corpus of Irish high crosses, as cited in the photograph's description.
cur:objects2-old-kilcullen-west-shaft.notes: The Entry into Jerusalem panel is small and weathered in the photograph; identification relies on Harbison. Material (granite) is assumed from the regional group and should be checked.

Q116274072.summary: On this fragment of carved tusk Christ sits frontally within an oval mandorla studded with ring-and-dot ornament, bearded and haloed, raising his right hand in blessing and holding a book in his left. Below him a winged angel reclines, appearing to support the mandorla. The stylised, patterned carving is characteristic of ivory work from early Islamic Egypt, where Christian communities continued to produce images of Christ in glory.
facts: The Met dates the fragment to 810–1010 and attributes it to Egypt (accession 17.190.48, gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917).
It is held in The Met's Department of Islamic Art, like the related tusk fragment with the Ascension (17.190.46), which shows a very similar enthroned Christ in a dotted mandorla.
Q116274072.notes: The relationship between the two Met tusk fragments is noted from their shared style, department and gift; whether they come from the same object was not verified.

walters:71.182.summary: Beneath three crocketed trefoil arches, Christ hangs on the cross with his head bowed and his knees bent, the Virgin bending in grief at the left and John, holding a book and resting his cheek on his hand, at the right. The sun and moon appear in the spandrels above. The pronounced sway of the figures is typical of Gothic ivory carving.
facts: The Walters singles out the unusually exaggerated bending pose of the Virgin.
Remains of broken silver hinges show that it was the right wing of a diptych, and an original diagonal hole at the top allowed it to be hung.
Henry Walters bought it in Paris in 1922.
walters:71.182.notes: Worklist year 800 was a parsing error for '3rd quarter 14th century'.

wga:m/master/zunk_sp/zunk_sp3/02crucif.summary: Christ hangs upright on an ivory cross, his head inclined, his large eyes wide open with dark inlaid pupils, and each foot nailed separately. The cross is alive with tiny figures and animals entwined in foliage; above the title board the risen Christ carries the cross, and at the foot Adam appears above the names of the donors, King Ferdinand and Queen Sancha. Given to San Isidoro in León, it is the earliest known Spanish crucifix bearing the figure of Christ.
facts: King Ferdinand I of León and Queen Sancha gave it to the basilica of San Isidoro in León; their names, FREDINANDUS REX and SANCIA REGINA, are carved at the foot.
It measures about 52 × 34.5 cm, and a small cavity behind Christ's body allowed it to serve as a reliquary.
On the back are the Lamb of God at the centre and the symbols of the four evangelists at the ends of the arms.

Q2067212.summary: Mary cradles the head of her dead Son while Mary Magdalene holds his feet and John flings his arms back in grief; above, angels wheel through the sky in anguish. Giotto gives his figures real weight and space, and uses a descending rocky ridge to lead the eye down to Christ's face. Two mourners seen only from behind draw the viewer into the circle of sorrow — a radical innovation in Western painting.
facts: The chapel was commissioned by the Paduan banker Enrico Scrovegni — according to a debated tradition, in atonement for usury; Dante placed his father Reginaldo among the usurers of the Inferno.
The small withered tree on the ridge is often read as nature itself mourning — and, like a tree that blossoms again in spring, as a hint of the Resurrection to come.
Giotto's cycle of some 37 narrative scenes covers the walls in tiers beneath a vault of deep blue, painted with costly ultramarine.
Visitors today wait about fifteen minutes in a climate-controlled chamber before entering, to lower humidity and filter out dust that could harm the frescoes.
